common_name: Benlehr Loquat (Compact Self-Fruitful Gulf Coast Loquat)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Benlehr's naturally compact 6-12 foot mature size makes it one of the more manageable loquat cultivars for a smaller Gulf Coast lot, and its self-fruitful habit means a single tree will set a crop without a second cultivar nearby.

directions: Benlehr is valued among Gulf Coast growers for staying noticeably smaller and more compact than standard loquat seedlings, topping out around 6 to 12 feet rather than the 15 to 25 feet many loquat trees eventually reach, which keeps the whole canopy within reach for pruning and harvest. It is self-fruitful, so an isolated dooryard tree still produces a reliable crop, though yields can improve slightly with a second cultivar such as Premier or Champagne planted nearby for cross-pollination. Fruit ripens over winter into early spring following the loquat's characteristic fall bloom, and like other loquat cultivars it should be thinned in heavy-set years to improve fruit size. Its smaller stature also makes Benlehr a practical choice for espalier training against a warm south-facing wall in the cooler parts of zone 8.
sources: Planting Justice — Benlehr Loquat variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Loquat Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers — Loquat Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Placentia is self-fertile and ripens later than most named loquat cultivars, so pair it with an early type like Advance if a long harvest window matters more than a single heavy late crop.

directions: Placentia traces back to seed introduced from Japan and planted in Placentia, California between roughly 1880 and 1900, making it one of the oldest named loquat selections still grown in the United States. It bears large, oblong to rounded fruit with tough orange-yellow skin dotted with numerous small white flecks, enclosing thick, firm, juicy orange flesh with a sweet, apricot-like flavor. Fruit is borne in small clusters of only a few loquats each rather than the large hanging trusses typical of some cultivars, and the thick skin lets Placentia fruit keep and ship better than thinner-skinned types. It ripens late in the loquat season and is self-fertile, so a single tree bears reliably on its own.
sources: University of California Riverside — Fruit & Nut Research and Information Center Loquat Fact Sheet
California Rare Fruit Growers — Loquat Fruit Facts

common_name: Early Red Loquat (Very Early-Ripening California Loquat)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Early Red is among the earliest-ripening named loquat cultivars, often coloring up in February, so protect the fall bloom and developing fruit from hard freezes since it is furthest along when winter cold arrives.

directions: Early Red is grown specifically to bring loquat harvest forward, with fruit commonly ripening as early as February in mild-winter climates, well ahead of standard-season cultivars such as Champagne or Premier. This early timing lets Gulf Coast and California growers plant it alongside a mid- or late-season cultivar to stretch the loquat harvest across several months rather than concentrating it into a few spring weeks. Because its fruit finishes developing during the coldest part of winter, Early Red is somewhat more exposed to freeze damage than later-ripening cultivars, so a warm microclimate against a south-facing wall improves consistency. Like other loquat cultivars it is self-fertile and benefits from thinning after a heavy bloom to improve fruit size.
sources: University of California Davis — Fruit & Nut Research and Information Center Loquat Fact Sheet
California Rare Fruit Growers — Loquat Fruit Facts

common_name: Argelino Loquat (Algerie Loquat, Spain's Leading Commercial Loquat)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Argelino ripens very early and blooms in fall like other loquats, so choose a warm, sheltered site to protect the developing fruit through winter.

directions: Also known as Algerie after its origin as an introduction from Algeria, Argelino has long been the dominant loquat cultivar of the Callosa d'en Sarria growing district in Alicante, Spain, where it and its bud-mutation offshoots account for the great majority of Spanish commercial loquat production. It ripens very early in the loquat season, bearing orange fruit that is notably high in sugar but carries enough tang to keep the flavor from tasting flat or one-dimensional. Several distinct bud sports have arisen from Argelino over the decades and are grown regionally under their own names, a testament to how widely the original selection has been propagated. In a home orchard it performs much like other Eriobotrya japonica cultivars, self-fertile and reliable, but is worth seeking out specifically for its early ripening and well-balanced sweet-tart flavor.
sources: International Society for Horticultural Science — Loquat in Spain: Production and Marketing (Acta Horticulturae 750)
CIHEAM — Loquat, Production and Market (Caballero & Fernandez)

common_name: Magoon Muscadine Grape (Self-Fertile Bronze Breeding-Stock Muscadine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or a container vine in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Magoon is self-fertile and needs a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis to support its vigorous growth.

directions: Released from Mississippi's muscadine breeding program, Magoon is a self-fertile bronze muscadine long grown in home gardens across the Gulf South for fresh eating, juice, and wine, and has also served as breeding stock in university grape-improvement programs, including as a parent of interspecific hybrid muscadine selections developed at the University of Florida. Vines are vigorous and productive once established on a strong trellis, ripening their bronze-gold berries through late summer alongside other classic self-fertile bronze cultivars like Carlos. As with other muscadines, Magoon shows strong natural resistance to Pierce's disease and the fungal diseases that trouble European bunch grapes in humid climates, so a home planting typically needs no fungicide program. Prune back hard to short spurs on permanent cordons each winter to keep the vine productive and manageable.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension Service — Establishment and Production of Muscadine Grapes
Mississippi State University Extension Service — What Varieties of Muscadines Should Be Grown

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Malayan Kumquat is noticeably less cold-hardy than Nagami or Meiwa kumquat, so Gulf Coast growers outside the mildest microclimates should grow it in a container that can be moved under cover for hard freezes.

directions: Native to Hainan Island in China and to Peninsular Malaysia, where it is known locally as limau pagar, this species is one of the least commonly grown kumquats in Western gardens and is distinguished by an unusually thin, smooth, aromatic peel relative to fruit size compared to the more familiar Nagami and Meiwa kumquats. Fruit is small and globose, roughly an inch across, ripening to a bright orange or golden-yellow and typically divided into four to six segments, and like other kumquats the sweet peel is eaten along with the tart pulp. The tree stays more compact and shrubby than standard kumquat cultivars, which suits container culture, but it is also more cold-sensitive, making it best suited to the warmest Gulf Coast microclimates or protected container growing rather than an unprotected zone 9a landscape planting. Its rarity outside botanical citrus collections makes it more of a specialty conversation piece than a mainstream dooryard fruit.
sources: Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection, University of California Riverside — Fortunella polyandra
Global Biodiversity Information Facility — Fortunella polyandra (Ridl.) Yu.Tanaka
